blocks.content: The Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable in nature, meaning they are not directly enforceable by courts for their violation.

rows: Conferred on citizens (and non-citizens in some cases)
Applicable exclusively to citizens of India

items: Fundamental Duties do not automatically carry legal sanctions; enforcement relies entirely on specific Parliamentary legislation.
The Verma Committee (1999) is frequently cited in exams regarding the legal identification and implementation of Fundamental Duties.
Failure to observe a Fundamental Duty cannot be challenged via writs under Article 32 or Article 226 unless a supporting law exists.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable, meaning citizens cannot be directly taken to court solely for failing to perform them.
Parliament has the legal authority to enforce Fundamental Duties by enacting specific penalizing statutes.
The Verma Committee (1999) identified existing legal provisions that enforce several Fundamental Duties.
Key statutes enforcing duties include the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act (1971) and the Wildlife Protection Act (1972).
Courts can refer to Fundamental Duties to determine the constitutional validity and reasonableness of a law.
